fields.question: Why study supervision at one or two positions in Sparse OPD?
fields.answer: Dense supervision may be redundant. Select important positive teacher–student differences to test concentration of useful information. A particular experiment doesn't prove one token suffices universally.
fields.example: Correcting one operator can matter more than imitating many connectives.

fields.question: Why aren't sparse loss and shorter generation the same efficiency improvement?
fields.answer: Sparse loss reduces supervised positions while keeping full trajectories and often scores them to find key tokens. Shorter generation changes cost and state coverage.
fields.example: Generating a thousand tokens and training one still pays for all generation.

fields.question: How distinguish unselected-token gradients from context?
fields.answer: Unselected positions have no direct loss but stay as conditioning; shared weights may still affect them. Local candidate tests aren't full Qwen/Llama training.
fields.example: Omitting step two's loss doesn't allow deleting it before scoring step three.

fields.question: Why retain full context while supervising only a few largest positive gaps?
fields.answer: Teacher distributions depend on actual preceding reasoning. Sparse gradients don't remove conditioning. Limited-position gains are setup-specific, and no local full-parameter distillation was run.
fields.example: Score one key correction with prior calculations intact; deleting the prefix changes the task.

fields.question: Why use fast and slow draft adaptation in SpecRoll?
fields.answer: RL changes target policy. Lightweight hidden corrections handle short drift; persistent degradation triggers future-head training. Both improve proposals without replacing target.
fields.example: Quickly adjust a transient acceptance drop, retrain the head only if it persists.

fields.question: Does changing the SpecRoll draft change GRPO target?
fields.answer: No. Exact target verification preserves sampling distribution, so GRPO stays unchanged. Skipping verification would change behavior data.
fields.example: Frequent correct drafts don't make their probabilities target policy probabilities.

fields.question: Does local SpecRoll registration prove large-model RL throughput?
fields.answer: No. Only states and selection paths are checked. Real work needs acceptance/rejection residuals, scheduling and compute measurements; listing isn't execution.
fields.example: A listed candidate does not demonstrate complete GPU training.

fields.question: Why can't fast correction or slow draft-head training replace exact verification?
fields.answer: They improve proposals as policy evolves; exact rejection/acceptance preserves target distribution. Skipping it changes RL data even with a strong drafter. No local large-model throughput evidence.
fields.example: Adapt the drafter after lag, but still verify every proposal.

fields.question: Why learn recoverability rather than just uncertainty in RAIL?
fields.answer: An uncertain state may be irreparable. Intervene based on expected recovery net of cost and condition on location/action, instead of uniformly spending extra.
fields.example: One missing tool retry and a fundamentally wrong premise have different recovery value.

fields.question: How does shadow-to-live evaluation differ from gold-based intervention choice?
fields.answer: Use permitted probes and actual feedback to learn recovery value. Gold would be an unavailable oracle. Deployment state must exclude training-only diagnosis.
fields.example: Restarting from a known solution plan is an oracle diagnostic, not a learned controller.

fields.question: What does the local RAIL path establish?
fields.answer: Reference intervention selection and cost objective, not the paper's LLMs, private environment or judges. Execute and evaluate real recoveries before capability/budget claims.
fields.example: Argmax over random recovery scores does not measure actual trajectory repair.

fields.question: Why optimize intervention location/method with cost instead of oversampling uncertain states?
fields.answer: Additional budget helps only recoverable states. Learn intervention-specific net gains from auditable shadow/live feedback as policy changes. Never use gold to decide; no local full environment.
fields.example: One more tool call can rescue a trace while no reasonable budget repairs a false premise; entropy alone can't tell.

fields.question: Why use pass@k to probe CoBA-RL boundaries before teacher help?
fields.answer: Pass@1 can increase by concentrating old successes. Larger-budget coverage finds currently difficult reachable edges, where teacher guidance supplies new routes for RL consolidation.
fields.example: Occasional successes becoming frequent differs from learning a previously unseen solution.

fields.question: How does a boundary curriculum differ from ranking fixed textual difficulty?
fields.answer: Reestimate from current policy samples; textual complexity doesn't track mastery. Finite k can miss rare successes, so boundary depends on budget and isn't impossibility.
fields.example: A long problem may leave the boundary after learning a new technique.

fields.question: Does local pass@8 establish paper pass@256 gains?
fields.answer: No. Teacher/student scales and sampling budgets differ. Genuine generation, triggers and cost curves support scaled mechanisms only.
fields.example: Failure in eight draws doesn't imply failure after over 200 draws.

fields.question: Why inspect both pass@1 and larger pass@k for capability boundaries?
fields.answer: First-hit gain may just popularize known paths. Multiple samples probe coverage, then teacher and RL target boundaries. Finite budgets still miss rare paths; local small sampling does not reproduce high-k expansion.
fields.example: Measure whether once-never-solved prompts become reachable with broader sampling, counting teacher cost.

fields.question: Why emphasize equal-label-budget stages in the sparse-to-dense reward principle?
fields.answer: Dense teachers have different supervision costs. Match label budgets and stages to understand ordering. Contribution is an empirical four-stage comparison, not another KL function.
fields.example: More teacher calls can improve scores without proving dense objectives caused the gain.

fields.question: Is the same KL direction equivalent on teacher and student occupancy?
fields.answer: No. Teacher ideal and student actual prefixes visit different errors. State source and divergence together define supervision.
fields.example: A KL on a correct proof and on a wrong intermediate state teaches different recovery.

fields.question: Do existing GRPO and OPD operators reproduce the four stages?
fields.answer: No. Literature only; no full scheduling, real frozen teacher or equal-budget runs. Shared tokenizer and other prerequisites still matter. Stage labels aren't execution.
fields.example: Listing four configuration stages does not validate their data flow.

fields.question: Why isn't the principle just sequencing GRPO and KL functions?
fields.answer: The paper tests four stages under equal label budgets and distinguishes forward KL on teacher-visited states from reverse KL on student states. Operators alone don't reproduce it. No local complete training.
fields.example: The same KL name on a teacher solution and a student error refers to different supervision.

fields.question: Why cache Lightning OPD teacher scores before updates?
fields.answer: Online teacher inference can bottleneck training. Score initial student traces once and reuse labels. This front-loads cost rather than eliminating generation/scoring.
fields.example: Prepare teacher scores per prefix and reread them for multiple updates.

fields.question: How does offline cache coverage differ from refreshing rollouts each step?
fields.answer: Cache covers initial student visits; updated policy may reach new states. Refreshing covers those at higher cost. Cached isn't always on-policy.
fields.example: A newly learned solution's prefixes won't appear automatically in an old cache.

fields.question: What Lightning cache identities must match?
fields.answer: Teacher checkpoint, prompt, tokenizer, response and position mask. Changes invalidate labels. Local data flow is not Qwen vocabulary distillation or AIME.
fields.example: A tokenizer update can misalign stored token scores despite the same filename.

fields.question: Why isn't cached teacher scoring equivalent to continuously online distillation?
fields.answer: Initial student samples are scored under one teacher config. Later updates shift visitation without refreshing labels. Coverage and teacher consistency govern the cost tradeoff; local evidence is data flow only.
fields.example: Cached early error prefixes help initially but later new approaches need an explicit refresh protocol.
